uncited: Intermixing operates on a sequence of ray samples where each sample $i$ consists of color and opacity values for $N$ distinct channels.
Let $c_{i,k}$ and $\alpha_{i,k}$ denote the color (RGB) and opacity (A) of channel $k$ at sample $i$, where $k \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
- A list of ray samples sorted front-to-back.
The standard front-to-back compositing loop is extended to handle multiple channels.
- **Complexity:** Time complexity is $O(R \cdot N \cdot S)$, where $R$ is the number of rays, $S$ is the number of samples per ray, and $N$ is the number of channels.
Memory complexity depends on the storage of $N$ channels per sample or brick.
Intermixing, specifically accumulation-level intermixing, was presented by Brix et al. in 2014 [BPH14] as part of an out-of-core rendering approach for multi-channel volume data sets.
It builds on Crassin et al.’s octree-based memory virtualization scheme [CNLE09].
The method is used in systems such as Voreen [DLJL22], Viv [MGP+22], and Neuroglancer [Goo22].
